title: SYSK Selects: How Twinkies Work
summary: A Saturday Selects rerun of the Stuff You Should Know episode "How Twinkies Work" (originally aired July 9, 2009). The hosts cover the Twinkie's origins at Continental Bakeries under James Dewar, who repurposed idle strawberry-filling machinery and named the cake after a billboard for Twinkle Toe shoes; the original banana cream filling replaced by vanilla during World War II shortages; the early egg-and-butter recipe with a two-day shelf life versus today's nine-ingredient formula with corn syrup, bleached flour, mono- and diglycerides, polysorbate 60, hydrogenated shortening and petroleum-derived artificial flavors; the factory baking process; shelf life claims including Hostess's 25-day figure and a Oregon schoolkids' nine-month buried-jar experiment; pop culture references such as Twinkie the Kid, the Twinkie defense in the Dan White trial, George Bellaire's Minneapolis bribery case, and the Millennium time capsule; Rice University's Twinkie tests (water, drop from a sixth-floor building, and a Turing test); and record-eaters. The episode closes with listener mail from Robin in Portland, Oregon, who was locked on a patio in Amsterdam and listened to the show while waiting for rescue.

segments.title: Opening banter and teasers
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Saturday Selects edition on Twinkies and the hosts joke around, teasing facts about Twinkie size, banana cream origins, and the snack's cultural status.

segments.title: Origins of the Twinkie
segments.summary: James Dewar of Continental Bakeries, a Hostess maker, repurposed idle strawberry-shortbread machinery to create a year-round yellow cake with cream filling; he named it after a Twinkle Toe shoes billboard. The original banana cream filling was dropped during World War II banana shortages and replaced by vanilla frosting.

segments.title: Early recipe versus modern ingredients
segments.summary: The early Twinkie was made with eggs, milk and butter and had a two-day shelf life. Today's version has nine ingredients including corn syrup, bleached wheat flour, mono- and diglycerides replacing eggs, polysorbate 60, hydrogenated shortening, and petroleum-derived artificial butter and vanilla flavors.

segments.title: Fan anecdotes and deep-fried Twinkies
segments.summary: The hosts swap memories of eating Twinkies, including a strawberry shortcake made with Twinkies, a Twinkie cookbook, and a deep-fried Twinkie recipe served at a beer festival.

segments.title: Factory baking and sealing process
segments.summary: Twinkies are baked upside down in metal molds at 350 degrees for nine to twelve minutes; the three holes are cream injection points, and the cakes are sealed airtight in packaging.

segments.title: Shelf life myths and the buried-jar experiment
segments.summary: Sorbic acid is the only ingredient added specifically as a preservative, and airtight packaging is key. Hostess says shelf life is 25 days. Two Oregon schoolkids buried a Twinkie-filled mayonnaise jar for nine months and found the cakes still edible.

segments.title: Twinkie pop culture: Twinkie the Kid and Twinkie Gate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Twinkie the Kid cowboy image and merchandise, then George Bellaire, a Minneapolis City Council candidate indicted for bribery after providing coffee, Kool-Aid and Twinkies to senior groups.

segments.title: The Twinkie defense
segments.summary: Dan White's 1979 killing of Harvey Milk and Mayor George Moscone in San Francisco; his defense argued depression and junk food binging, and he was convicted of manslaughter. The media coined the Twinkie defense, and Twinkies were named in court transcripts along with Ding Dongs and Ho Hos.

segments.title: Millennium time capsule and Twinkie in pop history
segments.summary: Bill Clinton selected a Twinkie for the Millennium time capsule alongside works by Louis Armstrong and William Faulkner and the Hawaii state flag.

segments.title: Rice University Twinkie experiments
segments.summary: Rice University students tested Twinkies in water, dropped them from a sixth-floor building, and ran a Turing test; the water test produced goo, the drop left a crack without major structural failure, and the Turing test found no sentience. The record for most Twinkies eaten is held by Lewis Browning, and James Dewar reportedly ate about 40,000.

segments.title: Closing thoughts
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the Twinkie episode with a final thought about moderation.
